chapter_note.about: Adversarial search is about games where two players take turns and want opposite things. Minimax gives every position a value by assuming the opponent always replies in the way that is worst for you. Alpha-beta pruning returns the same value while skipping branches that cannot matter, using two bounds called alpha and beta. How much it skips depends on the order in which moves are tried. Expectimax adds chance nodes for luck, which average their children instead of choosing. In the exam you fill a small tree, trace the pruning, or find the leaf values that make a subtree get pruned.

chapter_note.simple: Adversarial search is how a computer plays a two-player game like chess. It imagines the moves you could make and the replies your opponent could make, and it scores the endings. It assumes the opponent always replies in the way that hurts you most, and picks the move that still leaves you best off. Pruning is a shortcut: once you know a branch cannot beat something you already have, you stop reading it, and the answer stays the same. Games with dice add average squares to the picture. In exam words: minimax, alpha-beta pruning with its two bounds, move ordering, and expectimax with chance nodes.

cards.title: Minimax
cards.simple: Picture a two-player game like tic-tac-toe against a smart friend. You move, then your friend moves, and every possible ending gets a score: high is good for you, low is good for your friend. To pick your move, you assume your friend always answers in the way that hurts you most. So at your turns you take the biggest score, and at your friend's turns they take the smallest. Start at the endings and work backwards, and the number that reaches the top tells you how good the game is for you. In exam words: minimax, where MAX nodes take the largest child value and MIN nodes the smallest.
cards.idea: Two players take turns, and every ending has a score. You (MAX) want a high score and your opponent (MIN) wants a low one. To choose a move, assume the opponent always replies in the way that is worst for you. Fill the tree from the leaves up: a MAX node takes the **largest** child value, and a MIN node takes the smallest.
cards.idea_full: Take a game tree. Each node is a position, each edge is a move, and each leaf has a utility, a number saying how good that ending is for MAX. MIN's gain is MAX's loss, so MIN wants that number small. You cannot know what the opponent will do, so you plan for the worst reply. That makes the value of a position the score you can force, however well the opponent plays. At a MIN node the opponent picks, so the value is the smallest child. At a MAX node you pick, so the value is the largest child. Start at the leaves, fill one level at a time, and the root value is the score MAX can guarantee. The best move is the child that gave that value.
cards.definition:
$$V(n)=\max_{c\in \text{children}(n)}V(c)\ \text{(MAX node)},\qquad V(n)=\min_{c\in \text{children}(n)}V(c)\ \text{(MIN node)}$$

Symbols: V(n) is the minimax value of node n. At a leaf, V(n) is the utility written on it. 'children(n)' are the positions one move after n. The best move at the root is the child whose value equals V(root).
cards.intuition_full: Think of a chess player working out a forced line. She says: if I play this, my opponent's best answer is that, and then my best answer is this. Minimax does that for every line at once. Imagine each leaf as a price tag. MAX is a seller who wants the highest price he can force, and MIN is a buyer who wants the lowest. At each fork one of them chooses, and the choice always goes against the other. That is why a big number deep in the tree is worth nothing if the opponent controls the fork above it. Each fork squeezes its children to one number. The root is the last fork, and its number is what MAX is guaranteed.

example.setup: MAX moves first and chooses move b or move c. After each, MIN replies with one of three moves. The final utilities are: after b, 9, 5, 4. After c, 7, 6, 8. Find the minimax value of the root and MAX's best move.
steps: Label the levels. The root is MAX, b and c are MIN nodes, and the six numbers are leaf utilities.
MIN node b takes the smallest of 9, 5, 4. So b = 4.
MIN node c takes the smallest of 7, 6, 8. So c = 6.
MAX root takes the larger of b = 4 and c = 6. The value is 6, and the best move is c.
The biggest leaf, 9, sits under b. MIN would never allow it, so MAX does not chase it.
example.answer: Minimax value 6. The best move is c.

examples.setup: MAX has three strategies, 1, 2 and 3. After each, MIN picks one of three replies. The utilities after MIN's replies 1, 2, 3 are: strategy 1, (4, 10, 3). Strategy 2, (6, 2, 8). Strategy 3, (5, 5, 9). Both play optimally. Which strategy should MAX play?
steps: MIN moves second, so for each strategy MIN takes the row minimum.
Strategy 1: min(4, 10, 3) = 3.
Strategy 2: min(6, 2, 8) = 2.
Strategy 3: min(5, 5, 9) = 5.
MAX takes the best of the three row values: max(3, 2, 5) = 5, which is strategy 3.
The biggest number in the table, 10, is in strategy 1. MIN avoids it. The question asks for the strategy number (3), not the value (5).
examples.answer: Strategy 3, which guarantees a utility of 5.

examples.setup: This time the opponent moves first. The root is a MIN node. Its children d and e are MAX nodes. d has leaves 4 and 8. e has leaves 6 and 3. Find the value of the root.
steps: The root is MIN, so the bottom level is MAX. Start there.
MAX node d = max(4, 8) = 8.
MAX node e = max(6, 3) = 6.
MIN root = min(8, 6) = 6.
The name 'minimax' does not mean the root is MAX. The type of each node depends on who moves there. Using max at the root would give 8, which is wrong.
examples.answer: The root value is 6.

cards.why: Every game-tree question starts with this bottom-up fill, including pruning and expectimax. In GATE: you get a small tree or a table of utilities and must give the root value or the best first move.
how: Mark each level MAX or MIN, starting from the player who moves first at the root.
Write the leaf utilities.
Fill one level at a time, from the bottom: max at MAX nodes, min at MIN nodes.
The root value answers a question about the value. For the best move, pick the child that gave the root value.
Read the last line of the question again: value, move, or strategy number.

If two children tie for the best value, either is an optimal move. The question will state a tie-break if it needs one.
Leaves can sit at different depths. A leaf is just a value; the type of its parent decides how it is used.
If MIN plays badly, MAX gets at least the minimax value, never less.

cards.title: Minimax properties
cards.simple: Imagine a choose-your-own-adventure book where every page has 2 choices and the story is 3 pages long. To check every possible story you must read 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 endings. Add one more page and it doubles to 16. That is why long games get out of hand fast. The good news is that you only need to remember the page you are on and the choices you have not tried yet, not all the stories. And if the opponent plays perfectly, the best plan you find really is the best you can force. In exam words: minimax is complete on a finite tree, optimal against an optimal opponent, takes time O(b^m) and space O(bm).
cards.idea: Minimax checks every ending of the game. If each position has b moves and the game lasts m moves, that is b^m endings, so the time is **O(b^m)**. It goes depth first, so it only keeps one path and the waiting sibling moves in memory: **O(bm)**. On a finite tree it always finishes, and against a perfect opponent its move is the best possible.
cards.idea_full: Count the endings. With b choices at every one of m moves, the number of leaves is b times b times b, m times, which is b^m. Minimax has to score all of them, so its running time is O(b^m). That is exponential: for chess, with about 35 moves per position and games of about 100 moves, the number is far too large to ever finish. Memory is a different story. Depth-first search finishes one branch, throws it away and goes to the next, so only the current path and the unexplored siblings along it are stored. That grows like b times m. Two more facts are worth knowing. The search is complete: on a finite tree it always ends with a value. And it is optimal against an optimal opponent. If the opponent makes mistakes, MAX does at least as well as the minimax value says.
cards.definition:
$$\text{time}=O(b^{m}),\qquad \text{space}=O(bm)$$

Symbols: b is the branching factor, the number of moves from a typical position. m is the maximum depth, the number of moves until the game ends. Complete: on a finite tree minimax always returns a value. Optimal: against an optimal MIN it gets the best result MAX can force. If MIN errs, MAX gets at least that value.

Space is O(bm) if all successors of a node are generated at once, and O(m) if they are generated one at a time. The standard GATE answer is O(bm).
cards.intuition_full: Think of exploring a cave system with a ball of string. At every junction there are b tunnels, and every tunnel goes m junctions deep. To see every chamber you walk down every tunnel, which takes b^m trips. But the string only ever marks one route from the entrance to where you stand. That string is the memory, and its length is m junctions. Throw in a note for each tunnel you have not tried at each junction and you get b times m notes. The work explodes with depth because every new level multiplies the number of leaves by b. The memory barely grows because every new level adds only a path step and b notes. This gap between exponential time and tiny memory is why the fix for minimax is to cut time (pruning, depth limits), not memory.

example.setup: A game tree has branching factor b = 2 and depth m = 3. How many leaves must minimax score, and how much does depth-first minimax hold in memory at once?
steps: Each of the m = 3 moves has b = 2 choices, so the leaves number 2 × 2 × 2 = 2^3 = 8. The whole tree has 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 = 15 nodes.
Minimax goes depth first. It walks down one path, root, A, C, leaf. That is m + 1 = 4 nodes.
After scoring a leaf it backs up and forgets that branch. Only the current path and the siblings still waiting are kept.
At the end all 8 leaves were scored (time 2^3), but memory never held anything like the 15 nodes of the whole tree.
Add one level (m = 4): the leaves double to 2^4 = 16, but the path grows by only one node.
example.answer: Time is about b^m = 8 leaves. Memory is about b × m = 6 nodes, not 15. In general: O(b^m) time, O(bm) space.

examples.setup: A game tree has branching factor 10 and depth 4. Roughly how many leaves does minimax score? Roughly how many nodes does depth-first minimax store at once? What happens if the depth becomes 6?
steps: Memory = b × m = 10 × 4 = 40 nodes.
At depth 6: leaves = 10^6 = 1,000,000 and memory = 10 × 6 = 60 nodes.
Two more levels multiplied the work by 100 but added only 20 nodes of memory.
Trap check: memory is not b^m. Depth-first search never stores the whole tree.
examples.answer: About 10,000 leaves and 40 nodes at depth 4. At depth 6 it is 1,000,000 leaves and 60 nodes.

examples.setup: A MAX player follows minimax, but the MIN player is not optimal. At one MIN node with children valued 3 and 8, MIN picks the child valued 8 by mistake. Does MAX get less than, equal to, or more than the minimax value?
steps: Minimax assumed MIN would take the smaller child, 3. That is what the minimax value counted on.
MIN took 8 instead. For MAX, 8 is better than 3.
MIN can only help MAX by playing worse. The minimax value is MAX's guaranteed floor.
So MAX gets at least the minimax value, here 8 which is more than 3.
examples.answer: MAX gets at least the minimax value. Optimal means 'cannot do worse than the value', not 'always gets exactly the value'.

cards.why: The exponential time is the reason pruning exists, and the small memory explains why minimax runs depth first. In GATE: it can appear as statements to judge, such as 'complete', 'optimal against an optimal opponent', 'time O(b^m)' and 'space O(bm)'.
how: Count leaves with b^m: multiply b by itself m times.
Count memory with b × m. It is the current path plus waiting siblings.
Mark 'complete' only when the tree is finite.
Mark 'optimal' only against an optimal opponent.
Compare with BFS and DFS if asked: minimax is a depth-first search of the game tree.
cards.mistake: Writing space as O(b^m). That is the time. Depth-first minimax stores a path, not the tree, so its space is O(bm). The other slip is to say it is always optimal. It is optimal against an optimal opponent.
edge_cases: Infinite or looping games are not finite trees, so plain minimax may never finish. It needs a depth limit.
With a depth limit and an evaluation function at the cut-off, you get an estimate of the value, not the exact minimax value.
If successors are generated one at a time, memory drops to O(m). Check which one the question wants.
For chess, b is about 35 and m about 100, so b^m is about 35^100. This is the practical reason to prune.
connections: Foundations: Exponents and logarithms (b^m is a power, and each extra level multiplies by b).
Depth-first search memory is also O(bm); see Uninformed search: depth-first search.
Alpha-beta pruning (next cards) cuts the time without changing the answer.

cards.title: Alpha and beta
cards.simple: Picture a game show with two prize boxes. You have already opened box 1 and know it gives you at least 6 points. Now you start on box 2, but the host, who wants you to win as little as possible, picks the first outcome, and it is only 4 points. The host can only lower it from there, so box 2 can never beat box 1. You stop opening box 2 and save the effort. Alpha-beta keeps two running numbers: the best result you are already sure of (alpha) and the lowest result the opponent is already sure to hold you to (beta). When alpha reaches beta, you stop looking at that branch. In exam words: alpha is the highest value found so far for MAX on the path, beta is the lowest found so far for MIN, and we prune when alpha is at least beta.
cards.idea: While searching a game tree, keep two numbers. **Alpha** is the highest score MAX is already sure of. **Beta** is the lowest score MIN is already sure to hold MAX to. The value of the current node only matters if it falls between them. When alpha reaches beta (α ≥ β), that window is empty and the rest of the branch cannot change the answer.
cards.idea_full: Plain minimax reads every leaf. Alpha-beta carries two bounds down the tree so it can stop early. Alpha is the highest value MAX can already guarantee from choices made on the path from the root to here. It only goes up, and it starts at minus infinity. Beta is the lowest value MIN can already guarantee on that path. It only goes down, and it starts at plus infinity. Read them as a floor and a ceiling: the value of the current node only matters if it lands between alpha and beta. A MAX node raises alpha with each child it finishes. A MIN node lowers beta. When alpha meets or passes beta, one of the two players above already has a better option elsewhere. They would never walk into this node, so its unread children are skipped.
cards.definition:
$$\alpha=\text{highest value found so far for MAX},\qquad \beta=\text{lowest value found so far for MIN}$$

Updates: at a MAX node, α becomes max(α, child value). At a MIN node, β becomes min(β, child value). Start at the root with (α, β) = (−∞, +∞). Each child inherits its parent's pair.

Prune the remaining children as soon as α ≥ β. Equality counts.
cards.intuition_full: Imagine you are MAX and have found a route worth 6. That is your floor: whatever else happens, you can get 6. Now you open a second route, and its first outcome is 4 for you, because MIN controls this fork. MIN will pick at most 4 here. You already hold 6, so you will never choose this route. Reading the rest of it would be a waste, because MIN can only push it lower. This is the whole trick. Alpha is your floor. Beta is the ceiling that MIN has already managed to set. When the floor is at least the ceiling, there is no room left for the value to matter. The same logic runs mirrored for MIN, which is why a MAX node can be cut as well.

example.setup: Root A is MAX with MIN children B and C. B has leaves 6 and 9. C has leaves 4 and 8. Search left to right and track (α, β).
steps: Root A starts at (α, β) = (−∞, +∞) and passes that pair to B.
B reads leaf 6. B is MIN, so β = min(+∞, 6) = 6. B's pair is (−∞, 6).
B reads leaf 9: β = min(6, 9) = 6, unchanged. Check: −∞ ≥ 6 is false, no cut. B = 6.
A is MAX, so α = max(−∞, 6) = 6. A passes (6, +∞) to C.
C reads leaf 4: β = min(+∞, 4) = 4. Now α = 6 ≥ β = 4, so prune the leaf 8.
C is at most 4, so A = max(6, ≤4) = 6. Same as plain minimax.
example.answer: Root value 6. Leaf 8 is pruned because α = 6 ≥ β = 4 at C.

examples.setup: A MAX node is entered with (α, β) = (3, 8). Its children return the values 2, 5 and 9 in that order. Track α after each child. When does the node stop, and what does it return?
steps: Child 1 returns 2: α = max(3, 2) = 3. No change. Is 3 ≥ 8? No.
Child 2 returns 5: α = max(3, 5) = 5. Is 5 ≥ 8? No.
Child 3 returns 9: α = max(5, 9) = 9. Is 9 ≥ 8? Yes, so stop.
Any further children are skipped. The node returns at least 9.
Why it is safe: the MIN node above already has an option worth at most 8. It will never choose a node worth 9 or more.

cards.what: While searching a game tree, keep two numbers. **Alpha** is the highest score MAX is already sure of. **Beta** is the lowest score MIN is already sure to hold MAX to. The value of the current node only matters if it falls between them. When alpha reaches beta (α ≥ β), that window is empty and the rest of the branch cannot change the answer.
cards.what_full:
Plain minimax reads every leaf. Alpha-beta carries two bounds down the tree so it can stop early. Alpha is the highest value MAX can already guarantee from choices made on the path from the root to here. It only goes up, and it starts at minus infinity. Beta is the lowest value MIN can already guarantee on that path. It only goes down, and it starts at plus infinity. Read them as a floor and a ceiling: the value of the current node only matters if it lands between alpha and beta. A MAX node raises alpha with each child it finishes. A MIN node lowers beta. When alpha meets or passes beta, one of the two players above already has a better option elsewhere. They would never walk into this node, so its unread children are skipped.

$$\alpha=\text{highest value found so far for MAX},\qquad \beta=\text{lowest value found so far for MIN}$$

Updates: at a MAX node, α becomes max(α, child value). At a MIN node, β becomes min(β, child value). Start at the root with (α, β) = (−∞, +∞). Each child inherits its parent's pair.

Prune the remaining children as soon as α ≥ β. Equality counts.

**Worked example.** Root A is MAX with MIN children B and C. B has leaves 6 and 9. C has leaves 4 and 8. Search left to right and track (α, β).

1. Root A starts at (α, β) = (−∞, +∞) and passes that pair to B.
2. B reads leaf 6. B is MIN, so β = min(+∞, 6) = 6. B's pair is (−∞, 6).
3. B reads leaf 9: β = min(6, 9) = 6, unchanged. Check: −∞ ≥ 6 is false, no cut. B = 6.
4. A is MAX, so α = max(−∞, 6) = 6. A passes (6, +∞) to C.
5. C reads leaf 4: β = min(+∞, 4) = 4. Now α = 6 ≥ β = 4, so prune the leaf 8.
6. C is at most 4, so A = max(6, ≤4) = 6. Same as plain minimax.

**Answer:** Root value 6. Leaf 8 is pruned because α = 6 ≥ β = 4 at C.

cards.title: Tracing alpha-beta
cards.simple: Imagine choosing the best of three clubs to join. Each club's manager decides which offer you actually get, and he always picks his lowest, so a club is worth the lowest of its offers. You check club 1 and hear 6, 9 and 7, so it is worth 6. At club 2 you hear 8, then 5. The manager can now give you 5 at most, and you already have 6, so you walk out without hearing the last offer. At club 3 the first offer is 3, so you walk out at once. You heard only 6 of the 9 offers and still found the best club. In exam words: tracing alpha-beta means visiting leaves left to right, updating alpha and beta, and marking a subtree as pruned when alpha is at least beta.
cards.idea: To trace alpha-beta, visit the leaves from left to right and carry the pair (α, β) along. Each child starts with its parent's pair. When a node's bound crosses the bound above it, cross out the rest of that node's children. The order of the children decides how much you skip, but the root value never changes.
cards.idea_full: A trace is a table of bookkeeping. For every node you write the pair (α, β) it was entered with, then update it as children come back. A MAX node raises α. A MIN node lowers β. After every update ask one question: is α ≥ β? If yes, the node stops at once and returns what it has. The children it did not visit are pruned, along with all their descendants. Two things make traces go wrong. First, a bound only helps a branch that comes after it. The first MIN child of the root enters with α = −∞, so it can never be cut. Second, a cut only skips work. The values of pruned leaves do not matter, and the root value is the same as plain minimax. A cut can happen at a MIN node (an alpha cut, when β drops to α or below) or at a MAX node (a beta cut, when α rises to β or above).
cards.definition:
At every node, start with the (α, β) passed down by the parent.

MAX node: for each child, α = max(α, child value). If α ≥ β, stop and skip the rest.
MIN node: for each child, β = min(β, child value). If α ≥ β, stop and skip the rest.

Then return the node's value to the parent, and update the parent's α (if the parent is MAX) or β (if the parent is MIN). Children are visited left to right unless told otherwise.
cards.intuition_full: Think of the tree as a set of nested arguments. The root asks b: what can you get me? b answers 6. Then the root asks c, but tells c: I already have 6. c shows its first offer, 8, which is above 6, so c carries on. Its second offer is 5. Now c can promise nothing better than 5, and the root already holds 6. The root cuts c off mid-sentence. The cut does not need the rest of c's offers, because they can only be at most 5. This is why the pair is handed down. Without the 6 passed to c, c would have no reason to stop. With it, every MIN node under a MAX parent can stop as soon as one of its children is bad enough. The same story works upside down for a MAX node under a MIN parent.

steps: Root a starts at (α, β) = (−∞, +∞). Visit b first with that pair.
b reads 6, 9, 7. β = 6 after the first leaf and stays 6. Since α = −∞, no cut is possible. b = 6. Back at a, α = 6.

Root value = max(6, ≤5, ≤3) = 6. Leaves read: 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 of 9.
example.answer: Root value 6, the same as minimax. Six leaves are read. Leaf 10 (under c) and leaves 12 and 4 (under d) are pruned.

cards.title: Move ordering
cards.simple: Think of searching your bag for a pen. If the first thing you check is the pen pocket, you are done in one look. If you check every other pocket first, you search the whole bag. You find the same pen either way, but one search is much shorter. Alpha-beta is like that. It always finds the same answer as plain minimax, but if you look at the best moves first it can skip huge chunks of the game. If you look at the worst moves first, it skips nothing. In exam words: move ordering changes how many nodes alpha-beta examines, never the root value. The best ordering gives about b to the power m/2 leaves, and the worst gives no saving.
cards.idea: Alpha-beta always returns the same root value as minimax. What changes with the order of the children is how much work it skips. Look at the best move first and it prunes the most: about **b^(m/2)** leaves instead of b^m. Look at the worst move first and it prunes nothing.
cards.idea_full: A cut needs a bound that is already good. If the first child you search is the best one, α (or β) becomes strong straight away, and every later sibling is cut after a leaf or two. If the first child is weak, the bound is weak, and later children survive. In the best case, alpha-beta reads about b^(m/2) leaves, which is the square root of b^m. In the same time, it can search twice as deep as minimax. In the worst case it prunes nothing and reads every leaf, like minimax. In between, random ordering gives about b^(3m/4). None of this touches the answer: the root value and the best move are the same as plain minimax in every ordering. You cannot know the best move before searching, so real programs guess the order with heuristics, such as trying captures first or reusing the result of a shallower search.
cards.definition:
$$\text{best case: } O(b^{m/2}),\qquad \text{worst case: } O(b^{m}),\qquad \text{root value: always the minimax value}$$

Symbols: b is the branching factor and m is the depth, as in minimax. b^(m/2) is the square root of b^m. 'Best ordering' means that at every node the best child is searched first. 'Worst ordering' means that nothing is ever cut.
cards.intuition_full: Picture the bound as a bouncer. A strong bound turns most later children away at the door after one look. A weak bound lets them all in. The bound is only strong if the child you searched before it was strong. That is why the best move first matters so much. At every second level the first child is searched in full and its siblings are cut after a single look. Cutting at every other level is where the square root comes from. A tree that takes b^m leaves can be done in about b^(m/2), which is a square root. To halve an exponent is to double the depth you can afford. So good ordering buys twice the search depth for the same time.

example.setup: Root a is MAX with MIN children P, Q and R. Leaves left to right: P: 2, 6, 9. Q: 5, 7, 8. R: 6, 8, 7. Count the leaves alpha-beta reads in the order P, Q, R, and in the order R, Q, P. Compare the root values.

Order P, Q, R. P reads 2, 6, 9 with no bound yet: P = 2, α = 2. Q's leaves 5, 7, 8 are all above 2, so no cut: Q = 5, α = 5. R's leaves 6, 8, 7 are all above 5, so no cut: R = 6. All 9 leaves are read, and a = 6.
Now move R to the front: the order R, Q, P. Same tree, same numbers.
R reads 6, 8, 7: R = 6, α = 6 (3 leaves). Q's first leaf is 5, and 6 ≥ 5, so cut (1 leaf read). P's first leaf is 2, and 6 ≥ 2, so cut (1 leaf read). Total: 3 + 1 + 1 = 5 leaves.
Both orders give the root value 6. Order P, Q, R reads all 9 leaves. Order R, Q, P reads 5.
example.answer: The root value is 6 in both orders. Order P, Q, R reads all 9 leaves. Order R, Q, P reads 5.

examples.setup: A game tree has branching factor b = 4 and depth m = 6. How many leaves does minimax score? About how many does alpha-beta read with the best ordering? If minimax's leaf count is the time budget, how deep can best-ordered alpha-beta search?
steps: Best ordering: about b^(m/2) = 4^3 = 4 × 4 × 4 = 64 leaves. (The exact best case, 4^3 + 4^3 − 1 = 127, is of the same size.)
Saving: 4096 / 64 = 64 times fewer leaves.
Budget of 4096 leaves: solve 4^(m'/2) = 4^6, so m'/2 = 6 and m' = 12.
Worst ordering: no cuts. All 4096 leaves are read, the same as minimax. The root value is the same in all cases.
examples.answer: Minimax scores 4096 leaves. Best-ordered alpha-beta reads about 64. In the same budget it reaches depth 12, twice as deep.

At a MIN node, the best child to try first is the one with the smaller value (V = 8 beats U = 9). At a MAX node it is the larger.
examples.answer: The root value is 8 in both orders. Order U, V reads 4 leaves and order V, U reads 3.

cards.title: Pruning with unknown leaves
cards.simple: Suppose box 1 gives you 8 points for sure. For box 2, the host shows you a first number x and promises you will get at most x. When can you stop reading box 2? Exactly when x is 8 or less, because then box 2 can never beat box 1. If x is 9 or more, you must keep reading. So, instead of tracing with real numbers, you ask: for which x does my stop-rule fire? You write the rule as a small inequality with x in it and solve it. In exam words: write the pruning test alpha at least beta with the unknown leaf inside it, then solve for the range of that unknown.
cards.idea: Sometimes a leaf is a letter, not a number, and the question asks: for which values is a subtree pruned? Trace the tree up to that leaf and write down the current α and β. The pruning test α ≥ β then turns into an **inequality** in the unknown. Solve it. Equality prunes, so the boundary value is included.
cards.idea_full: A cut depends on a comparison between two bounds. When one of the bounds is an unknown leaf x, the comparison becomes an inequality. For example, a MAX root already holds α = 8 from its left child. Its right child B is a MIN node whose first leaf is x. After reading x, β = x. The next leaf of B is pruned when α ≥ β, that is when 8 ≥ x. So the leaf is pruned for every x up to and including 8. If two unknowns appear, trace in order and write one condition for each cut. Often the condition contains a min or a max, such as α = min(9, y). Replace the min by its parts: min(9, y) ≥ 6 holds when 9 ≥ 6 (always true) and y ≥ 6.
cards.definition:
$$\text{prune when } \alpha\ge\beta$$

To find a range: (1) find α at the moment the target node is entered, (2) find β after the unknown leaf is read, (3) write α ≥ β (or the mirrored test at a MAX node), (4) solve for the unknown, keeping the equality.

With a min or a max inside: min(p, y) ≥ c means p ≥ c and y ≥ c. And min(p, y) ≤ c means p ≤ c or y ≤ c.
cards.intuition_full: Think of the number line. The bound α is a point on it. The unknown x can sit anywhere on the line. The cut happens when x lands on one side of α, including α itself. So the answer is always a half-line: everything up to α, or everything from α upwards. Which side it is depends on who is cutting. A MIN node (under a MAX parent) is cut when its value falls to α or below, so the pruned range is x ≤ α. A MAX node (under a MIN parent) is cut when its value rises to β or above, so the range is x ≥ β. Draw the point and the half-line before you write the inequality. That one picture prevents the common mistake of getting the direction wrong.

example.setup: Root A is MAX. Its left child is a leaf worth 8. Its right child B is a MIN node whose leaves are x (first) and 2 (second). For which values of x is the leaf 2 pruned?
steps: Search the left child first. The leaf 8 gives α = 8. B is entered with (α, β) = (8, +∞).
B reads x first, so β = min(+∞, x) = x. The second leaf is pruned when α ≥ β, that is 8 ≥ x.
Test x = 5: β = 5, and 8 ≥ 5 is true, so the leaf 2 is pruned.
Test x = 11: β = 11, and 8 ≥ 11 is false, so the leaf 2 is read.
Boundary x = 8: 8 ≥ 8 is true, so the leaf is pruned. Equality counts.
So the leaf 2 is pruned exactly when x ≤ 8.
example.answer: The leaf 2 is pruned for x ≤ 8, that is x in (−∞, 8].

cards.title: Expectimax
cards.simple: Think of a board game with a dice roll. You can't plan against the dice like you plan against a clever friend, because the dice just do whatever they do. So you ask: on average, how good is this move? If a move gives 12 points a quarter of the time and 4 points the other three quarters, its average is 0.25 × 12 + 0.75 × 4 = 6. You work out the average for each move and pick the best one. Dice squares in the tree are 'take the average' squares, and your own squares are still 'take the best'. In exam words: expectimax, where chance nodes take the probability-weighted average of their children and MAX nodes take the maximum.
cards.idea: Some games include luck: dice, shuffled cards, a random event. In the tree, luck is a **chance node**. Nobody chooses there. Its value is the **average** of its children, each weighted by its probability. MAX nodes still take the largest value and MIN nodes the smallest. Fill the tree from the leaves up, as in minimax.
cards.idea_full: A chance node stands for nature, not for a player. Each outgoing edge carries a probability, and the probabilities at a node add to 1. The value of the node is the expected utility: multiply each child's value by its probability and add. That is a weighted average, so a rare big outcome counts for little and a likely small one counts for a lot. Everything else is as in minimax. A MAX node takes the largest child. A MIN node takes the smallest. Expectimax uses the sizes of the utilities, not just their order. If you replace every utility by its square root, minimax picks the same move, but expectimax may pick a different one. Pruning is harder too. Alpha-beta cuts a node when it knows the rest cannot matter, but an unseen child of a chance node could still shift the average. So pruning chance nodes needs bounds on the possible leaf values.
cards.definition:
$$V(n)=\sum_i p_i\,V(c_i)\qquad\text{(chance node with children }c_i\text{)}$$

Symbols: p_i is the probability of the i-th outcome, and the p_i at one chance node add to 1. V(c_i) is the value of the i-th child. MAX nodes take max V(c). MIN nodes take min V(c). The root value is the best expected utility MAX can get.
cards.intuition_full: Compare two gambles by playing each a thousand times and writing down the average winnings. That average is the expected value, and it is the fair way to rank them. The chance node does the same sum in one go: each outcome contributes its value times how often it happens. A gamble that pays 12 once in four plays and 4 otherwise averages 6, even though 12 looks tempting. A rival gamble that pays 7 or 5 most of the time averages 6.2, and wins. MAX then chooses between the averages like a normal max node. The main difference from minimax is who is in control. At a MIN node an opponent is choosing against you, so you plan for the worst. At a chance node nobody is choosing, so you plan for the average.

example.setup: MAX chooses action L or action R. After L, a chance node gives utility 12 with probability 0.25 and utility 4 with probability 0.75. After R, a chance node gives 7 with probability 0.6 and 5 with probability 0.4. Find the expectimax value of the root and the best action.
steps: Check the weights. 0.25 + 0.75 = 1 and 0.6 + 0.4 = 1. Good.
MAX takes the larger: max(6, 6.2) = 6.2. The best action is R.
The biggest utility, 12, is under L but has only a 25% chance. The probabilities decide.
example.answer: The root value is 6.2, and MAX plays R.

What is the expectimax value, and which action does a pessimist choose who treats each chance node as a MIN node?
steps: Check the weights. 0.5 + 0.3 + 0.2 = 1 and 0.7 + 0.3 = 1.
Expectimax: max(8, 6.5) = 8, so play L.
Pessimist: L = min(8, 0, 20) = 0 and R = min(5, 10) = 5. The pessimist plays R.
The two rules disagree. That is what the question is testing.

examples.setup: Action A leads to a chance node: 64 with probability 0.5 and 0 with probability 0.5. Action B leads to a sure 25. Which does expectimax pick? Then replace every utility by its square root and ask again.
steps: Before: A = 0.5 × 64 + 0.5 × 0 = 32 + 0 = 32. B = 1 × 25 = 25. Expectimax picks A.
Take square roots. 64 becomes 8, 25 becomes 5, and 0 stays 0. The order of the outcomes is unchanged: 0 < 5 < 8.
After: A = 0.5 × 8 + 0.5 × 0 = 4. B = 1 × 5 = 5. Expectimax now picks B.
The decision flipped although the order of the outcomes did not. Expectimax depends on the sizes of the utilities. Minimax uses only comparisons, so such a change cannot alter its decision.
examples.answer: Expectimax switches from A (32 against 25) to B (4 against 5). Minimax would not change.

steps.caption: MAX moves first and picks b or c. MIN then picks one of three replies. The six numbers at the bottom are final utilities. Fill in values from the bottom up.
MIN node b takes the smallest of 9, 5 and 4. So b = 4.

scenes.title: Alpha and beta as a shrinking window

steps.caption: Root A starts with the widest window: α = −∞ (MAX is sure of nothing yet) and β = +∞ (MIN is sure of nothing yet).
A passes the same pair down to B. B reads leaf 6. B is MIN, so β = min(+∞, 6) = 6. α is untouched.
Leaf 9: β = min(6, 9) = 6, no change. Is α ≥ β? −∞ ≥ 6 is false, so there is no cut. B returns the value 6.
Back at A, a MAX node: α = max(−∞, 6) = 6. A now guarantees at least 6. It passes (6, +∞) down to C.
C reads leaf 4. C is MIN, so β = min(+∞, 4) = 4. Now α = 6 and β = 4, so α ≥ β. MIN could hold A to at most 4 here, but MAX already has 6. Leaf 8 is pruned.
C returns at most 4, so A = max(6, ≤4) = 6. Same answer as plain minimax, with one leaf never read.
Root a is MAX. b, c and d are MIN nodes. Children are searched left to right. The root starts at (α, β) = (−∞, +∞).
b inherits (−∞, +∞). Leaf 6 gives β = 6. Leaves 9 and 7 do not lower it. α is still −∞, and −∞ ≥ 6 is false, so no cut: all 3 leaves are read. b = 6.
Back at a, a MAX node: α = max(−∞, 6) = 6. c starts with (6, +∞). Leaf 8 gives β = 8. Is 6 ≥ 8? No, so keep reading.
Leaf 5 gives β = min(8, 5) = 5. Now 6 ≥ 5, so cut. Leaf 10 is never read. c is at most 5.
d starts with (6, +∞). Its first leaf is 3, so β = 3 and 6 ≥ 3: cut at once. Leaves 12 and 4 are never read. d is at most 3.
Root: a = max(6, ≤5, ≤3) = 6, and the best move is b. Only 6 of 9 leaves were read, and the value equals plain minimax.

scenes.title: Move ordering changes the work, not the answer

steps.caption: Root a is MAX with three MIN children, searched left to right in the order P, Q, R. The leaves are P: 2, 6, 9. Q: 5, 7, 8. R: 6, 8, 7.
Order P, Q, R. P reads 2, 6, 9 (no bound yet, no cut): P = 2, α = 2. Q reads 5, 7, 8, all above 2: Q = 5, α = 5. R reads 6, 8, 7, all above 5: R = 6. No cut anywhere. All 9 leaves are read and a = 6.
Now put R first. The tree is the same and so are the numbers. Only the order of the children changes: R, Q, P.
Order R, Q, P. R reads 6, 8, 7: R = 6, α = 6. Q's first leaf is 5, and 6 ≥ 5, so cut: 7 and 8 are skipped. P's first leaf is 2, and 6 ≥ 2, so cut: 6 and 9 are skipped. Only 5 leaves are read.
Both orders give the root value 6. The order changed the work from 9 leaves to 5. Trying the best move first is what makes pruning pay.
